posts.name: Hamilton
posts.text:
What do $RBLX $DUOL $HIMS $HOOD and countless others have to do with $NBIS $IREN $ASTS $ONDS ??

They've all topped for this cycle and will eventually draw down 80-90% at least.

They're all products of liquidity + narrative + human insanity. 

We talked about this for an hour today inside our Discord.

Markets do not move on valuations, future projections, or dudes with 1 million followers and 4,700 word long tweets about why some shit space company in the middle of the usa is going to outperform a trillion dollar $SPCX.

They move because people buy. Then the media drums up a story to justify rising prices. Which makes more people buy. Which makes the media continue to drum up stories to justify rising prices. 

And then.. it pops. And you get the exact opposite effect: prices draw down, narratives are invented to justify, people sell more/shorts hop on, narratives continue to justify falling prices, until the stock is worth less than 10% of what it was at all-time highs.

The memory/photonic/neocloud team is no better than the ape bois who still cry about $GME and $AMC -- just a diff story with a diff boogey man.

Markets are tough. Use a stop loss.

$ANT ANT IS HEAVY, AND SOME OF THE SHORTS ARE PROBABLY THE OWNERS

Anthropic debuted today into the weakest tape of the year for the AI complex, and the stock has been under pressure from the open. The easy read is that the market is rejecting the valuation. There is a mechanical explanation that fits better, and it starts with who owned this company before today.

Anthropic's cap table is not only institutions. Across years of private rounds, secondary sales and SPVs, a long tail of private individual investors holds pre-IPO stock, in many cases sitting on windfalls of ten to fifty times their money. As of this morning those windfalls are marked to market, and most of them cannot be sold. The lockup runs up to a full year.

A holder in that position has an obvious trade available: short the listed stock against the locked shares, or buy puts once options list, and the paper windfall becomes a locked gain whatever the next year brings. Every point the stock falls from here pays out on the hedge against shares the holder cannot sell until 2027.

Three frictions stand in the way, and they explain why this is pressure rather than a flood. The lockup bars hedging until day 195, June 1, 2027, and then allows only 20% of a holder's remaining restricted shares. A short against the box is a constructive sale for tax purposes, so the gain is taxed as if it were realized. And borrow in a float of about 7% is scarce, expensive and recallable.

But detection is not one of the frictions. Short interest is published twice a month as a single aggregate number with no names attached. No filing identifies a small holder's short. The company and the underwriters, the parties to the lockup, have no window into anyone's brokerage account. For thousands of small private holders, nobody would know.

So some of the early short interest in this name will not be bears betting against Anthropic. It will be owners insuring windfalls they are not allowed to sell. The footprints to watch are the first published short interest print in mid-December, the put skew once ANT options list, and the release dates below, starting December 15, which test how much eligible stock actually gets sold by holders who could not hedge.

The reason the incentive lasts is the schedule itself. Here it is in full.

THE LOCKUP THAT CREATES THE INCENTIVE

Anthropic priced at $83 with about 980M shares in public hands, roughly 7% of the 13.09B shares outstanding. Behind that float sit about 15.5B restricted shares, options and awards, and they do not free up on one date. The prospectus sets 23 release dates across a full year, keyed partly to fixed day counts and partly to earnings reports. Every figure below is an eligibility ceiling. The filing does not say any holder intends to sell.

THE TWO TRACKS

About 2.7B shares, held by employees, non-founder directors and officers, and a group of other stockholders, are restricted for up to 180 days, ending at the earlier of two trading days after Q1 2027 results or May 17, 2027.

About 8.0B shares, held by the seven co-founders and the larger stockholders above 0.5%, are restricted for up to 365 days, ending at the earlier of two trading days after Q3 2027 results or November 18, 2027.

THE RELEASE CALENDAR

Day one, November 19, 2026: up to 316M shares, the non-founder insiders' 10% allowance. The CFO and chief accounting officer are named in the filing as eligible to sell from the first session.

December 15, 2026 and January 5, 2027: up to 299M on each date. 914M cumulative.

January 19 and February 2, 2027: up to 349M on each date. 1.61B cumulative, about twice the shares sold in the offering as filed.

Second trading day after FY2026 results: up to 1.7B. 3.31B cumulative. This step carries the insiders' further 35% release.

13, 27, 41, 55 and 69 days after FY2026 results: up to 474M on each date. 5.68B cumulative.

posts.text:
🚨 Séance très violente sur Wall Street

Personne dans l'IA n'a envie de lire ce qui suit mais lisez-le quand même

Quelques explications :

1. Anthropic lève 81,3 Md$ et aspire la liquidité

IPO à 83 $, premier échange à 111,50 $, plus haut vers 115 $, vers 96 $ à 15h10. Plus de 2 000 Md$ de valorisation à l'ouverture, 80% des salariés deviennent millionnaires sur le papiers, dont 400 avec + de 100M.

La lecture qui domine est que pour acheter de l'ANT, les gérants ont vendu les Mag 7 et les semis. Pas d'entrée au Nasdaq-100 avant le 18 décembre, donc aucun achat indiciel pour compenser. $AMZN plus grosactionnaire, perd 3,9 %, Google pareil.

L'IPO se pase comme une IPO standard, open très haut, beaucoup de ventes de prise de profits, puis souvent une consolidation. Le consensus US était d'acheter la pré-ipo et la vendre directement, je ne suis donc absolument pas surpris. 

2. Google accélère et des rumeurs folles d'AGI

Gemini 4 Neon est sorti hier : 61 sur l'index d'Artificial Analysis, 3e au classement, 3 $ le million de tokens. La rumeur parle d'un petit modèle entraîné avec de l'auto-amélioration récursive, et le DeepMind Institute publie un essai qui décrit l'AGI comme « à portée ». Un modèle aussi bon et moins cher pèse sur le prix des tokens, $GOOGL passe de +4,1 % à -2,8 % cependant

Google est connu pour faire du Benchmaxxing à l'inverse de Grok mais je ne vous cache pas que pour le coup là c'est extrêmement intéressant. Time to AGI : 0 ? 

3. AMD a désormais son propre problème chinois

Hunterbrook se déclare short $AMD : IEIT, fabricant chinois de serveurs sur liste noire, aurait intégré au moins six versions récentes de son firmware. 

Hunterbrook reconnaît n'établir aucune violation, AMD conteste. Le titre perd 9,4 %, le jour où la règle du Commerce sur Singapour (12,4 % du CA 2025) entre en vigueur. Ma lecture c'est que ça amplifie une news déjà bien salée, mais je ne pense pas qu'il y ait un problème sur AMD.

4. TSMC coupe une partie de la Chine, les semis rendent tout

TSMC et Samsung suspendent certaines livraisons à des clients chinois en attendant les licences du Commerce. Cela à surpris le $SOX de +4,7 % à -2,3 %, $NVDA de +4,75 % à -2,7 %, $MU de +7,8 % à -1,9 %. Nvidia file vers une sixième baisse d'affilée, $NBIS lâche 8,8 %, les neoclouds sont vraiment en enfer...

5. Le consensus shift doucement vers une capitulation

VIX vers 28, $QQQ sous son plus bas du 17 novembre. Les gens rangent les armes jusqu'à janvier, l'IPO d'Anthropic devait être un signal positif

Je ferait un post plus long pour expliquer ce que je retiens de mon voyage aux USA, après avoir parlé à des buyside & sell side. Meh.

6. Les rares îlots verts

Palo Alto +5,2 % après ses résultats et le rachat d'Applied Compute, $PDD +10,9 %. $BABA a touché +4,5 % avant de repasser dans le rouge. Le reste se fait juste enterrer.

7. Roaring Kitty est de retour

Il revient avec un meme Nintendo. Nintendo prend 15 % et $GME 7 % sur la news, hilarant mais je me tiendrai bien à l'écart

Demain je surveille $ANT face aux 83 $ de l'IPO, les suites sur $AMD et les licences pour TSMC, le KOSPI risque de déguster cette nuit

$VVV KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM VALVOLINE’S FISCAL Q4 2026 EARNINGS CALL

Valvoline’s November 19, 2026 call supports selective industry conclusions rather than a broad consumer-recovery thesis. Comparable sales increased 9.4%, but same-store transactions were approximately flat, finished-lubricant costs increased approximately 60%, and pricing principally protected profit dollars rather than margins. The strongest positive implications concern producers benefiting from constrained premium base-oil supply and aftermarket distributors serving vehicles that consumers retain longer. The strongest negative implications concern automotive-service operators exposed to customer-acquisition costs, delayed maintenance spending, and development bottlenecks. The critical distinction is between essential demand and profitable growth: maintenance remains necessary, but that does not ensure rising transactions, unrestricted pricing power, or expanding margins. The implications below distinguish confirmed exposure from inferred earnings effects and near-term catalysts from longer-duration changes.

ENERGY: BASE OILS AND LUBRICANTS

PREMIUM BASE-OIL SCARCITY SUPPORTS PRODUCER EARNINGS LONGER THAN CRUDE-PRICE SIGNALS SUGGEST (READ-THROUGH 1)

Affected companies: S-Oil (010950: South Korea) and SK Innovation (096770: South Korea). Direction: positive. Magnitude: high for the lubricant businesses and material for consolidated earnings, particularly at S-Oil. Conviction is high in the direction of the near-term supply-and-margin transmission, but not in extrapolating record quarterly profits indefinitely.

The strongest supporting commentary is Valvoline’s confirmation that finished-lubricant costs increased approximately 60%, remained elevated, and had stabilized rather than declined. Management’s fiscal 2027 outlook assumes that this environment persists. Willis emphasized that “the base oil market and the crude oil market don’t necessarily run-in tandem,” while Flees explained that the constraint is “not just about oil flow, it’s also about refining capacity.” This directly challenges the assumption that lower crude prices or improved crude availability should quickly reverse premium base-oil economics.

The transmission mechanism is scarcity pricing on saleable base oils relative to feedstock and operating costs. Producers with available, qualified Group III capacity can retain stronger realized spreads while disrupted competitors remain unable to supply customers. Valvoline’s continued premium-lubricant mix growth and absence of meaningful trade-down indicate that downstream customers have not broadly substituted away from the constrained product category. That supports the persistence of demand for available premium base oils even as finished-lubricant prices rise.

The producers’ already-reported results establish that this is economically substantial rather than a theoretical commodity exposure. S-Oil’s November 2 earnings call reported Q3 lubricant operating profit of KRW 742.7 billion, approximately 53% of total operating profit of KRW 1,406.7 billion. Its disclosed base-oil spread reached $166.8 per barrel, and management expected continued supply tightness in Q4. SK Innovation’s October 29 disclosure reported KRW 1,090.6 billion of operating profit at SK Enmove, compared with KRW 3,704.3 billion of consolidated operating profit. These figures demonstrate the scale of lubricant exposure, although subsidiary operating profit should not be translated directly into attributable parent-company EPS without ownership and consolidation adjustments.

Valvoline’s incremental information is therefore confirmation from a large downstream purchaser that the scarcity had not meaningfully unwound by mid-November. posts.text:
When I first got hired at Merrill, right at the end of the financial crisis, my manager told me straight out:

I didn't hire you for your IQ. I hired you for your EQ.

Pissed me off at the time.. but looking back at it now over a decade later I realize it was a gift.

The last nearly 2 decades has taught me that you don't have to be the smartest in the room to make money in the markets.

As a matter of fact the smartest guys tend to be the biggest losers.

Too much brains. Not enough shutting the hell up and listening to when the market tells them they are wrong.

Plenty of those types this year on FinTwit.. watching life changing amounts of money fade away as their portfolio drops 85-90% in the matter of a couple of months.

I don't think I'm smarter than Wall Street. And I never have.. so I don't try to outsmart everyone.

I look at where the big funds are positioning, where they're placing their money.. and I make a choice to either buy, sell or wait.

That's 95% of my job. Following capital flows and waiting. And it's worked well for me over the last decade.

Here's a great example from this morning..

Our trading room is short gold via some $GLD puts. I posted about it a few days ago on here and over the last three days the trade has worked out well.

Gold is down about 5% and my $GLD puts are up over 100%.

I took some profits and updated the post. That really pissed one guy off.

I'm a dumb fuck because I didn't open the short position when gold was at all-time highs.

Maybe he's right. I would've made a lot more money. But I didn't. I chose to wait for Wall Street to line up with my thesis, the chart to give me an entry, and an opportunity to put the trade on.

I hope to be as good as Error 404: Brain Not Found one day. Until then, I'll be the guy who happily admits to not being the smartest in the room.. as long as I am making money.

posts.text:
Palo Alto Networks is paying $4.5 billion for a 70-person AI company.

Applied Compute doesn't sell security. It customizes open-weight models on each company's own data and runs them.

Three things stood out to me about the deal:

1️⃣ The team.

Its founders worked on Codex, O1 and reinforcement learning at OpenAI.

Management said no other team came close in post-training open-weight models.

2️⃣ The customers.

Microsoft, DoorDash, Harvey in legal and Decagon in customer service already use it.

NVIDIA is both a customer and an investor.

Its revenue passed a $100M annual run rate within 18 months of founding.

3️⃣ The price.

Two weeks earlier, Applied Compute raised at a $3.25B valuation.

By our math, Palo Alto is paying ~40x revenue, net of ~$500M in cash and prepaid compute.

Why would a security company buy a model builder?

Palo Alto's view is that you can't supervise AI without knowing how to train it.

It also sees serving secure open models to enterprises as a market worth hundreds of billions.

Expected close: Feb–Apr 2027.

Comment "PANW" and I'll send you our notes on the deal.

posts.text: My honest takeaway from this week is that the momentum trade still has plenty of room to just keep sliding down. Crowd is right most of the time. posts.text:
🚨 $ONDS | FCC Votes to Release More Spectrum for the Skies

The FCC adopted final rules today, affecting three spectrum changes for drones and air mobility.

🔹 450 MHz:  Opened for safety-related data links between ground and crewed/uncrewed aircraft, replacing old site-by-site rules with a nationwide licensing system.

🔹 24.45–24.65 GHz:  Ground-based radar systems can now use this band to detect and track unauthorized or dangerous drones near airports, borders, prisons, stadiums, and critical infrastructure.

🔹 800 MHz:  Air-to-ground band rules updated so providers can deliver modern in-flight broadband to commercial and other aircraft.

What does this mean for companies like $ONDS?

➡️ The 24 GHz piece is the most relevant… it gives $ONDS’s C-UAS products a licensed spectrum ‘home’ for the detection side of their deployments. The release frames it as detection and tracking only (no jamming or takedown authority).

➡️ The 450 MHz nationwide licensing also helps $ONDS’s own drone operations, since its aircraft need licensed data links to fly.

quoted.text:
Two things about IPOs:

1/ There's usually a rally on the first day. 

This is known as the "first day pop" effect and it's largely caused by IPO mispricing and investor hype.

Barron's noted that the average 1D gain for IPOs this year was something like 15%.

2/ IPOs typically underperform in their first 1-3 years. Ritter (1991), "The Long-Run Performance of Initial Public Offerings." 

So very often you'll see a nice pop then some prolonged consolidation. They don't have to last 3 yrs especially in a hot market.

This creates a nice "base breakout" setup for IPOs, and I've personally found that to be the best way to trade them.

quoted.text:
Some Color Through the Minervini Lens
Subject: $SPY, $DIA short positions initiated on 10/15 and doubled on 11/11.

I’m now sitting on a 5R profit relative to my original risk, meaning I’ve made five times what I initially risked. That great for two reasons: 1. I've made a worthwhile gain. 2. It opens up options.
I can simply take the profit. 5-to-1 reward-to-risk is an excellent trade and certainly well worth the effort.  
Or I can move my stop to breakeven, give the position some room, and play it for a potentially much bigger move, having open-ended profit potential with zero risk.
That's exactly where I am now. The profit I've built allowed me to move my stop to breakeven and effectively eliminate the original risk. I've earned the right to play for the bigger move, working my way into the best situation possible; a profitable freeroll.
And that's the key. I don't enter a trade and immediately decide that I'm going to hold out for some pre-determined target or enormous move regardless of what happens. First, the trade has to prove itself. If it moves sufficiently in my favor and gives me an opportunity to de-risk the position, then I can decide whether to take the profit or give it time to develop into something more.
That's how you put yourself in position for asymmetric leverage: start with small risk, let the trade earn its way, improve your worst-case scenario, eliminate the risk when the opportunity presents itself, and then give the bigger move a chance to happen ri

HUNTERBROOK REPORTS $AMD FIRMWARE APPEARED IN SOFTWARE UPDATES FROM A U.S.-BLACKLISTED CHINESE SERVER MAKER

Hunterbrook's new investigation into AMD found that IEIT Systems, a Chinese server manufacturer blacklisted by the U.S. in March 2025, continued posting server software updates containing newer AMD firmware after the restrictions took effect.

Key findings:

• Firmware updates: IEIT posted at least six server BIOS updates containing newer versions of AMD's firmware after being blacklisted, including an update posted October 19, 2026.

• Linked companies: Hunterbrook found that three other server vendors, Aivres, Kaytus and Maginfra, published firmware files that were 99.94% identical to IEIT's. Kaytus identifies IEIT as its ultimate parent.

• AI chips: AMD's own website lists Aivres as a partner offering servers powered by its Instinct AI accelerators, including the MI300X and MI325X.

• China revenue: AMD generated $7.75B, or 22.4% of its 2025 revenue, from customers billed in China and Hong Kong.

• Supply chain: Two Chinese joint ventures controlled by Tongfu Microelectronics perform most of AMD's chip assembly, testing and packaging. AMD purchased roughly $2B in services from them in 2025.

AMD did not answer Hunterbrook's questions about whether it held export licenses for the companies involved.

The investigation does not establish that AMD violated export laws or determine how IEIT obtained the firmware.

posts.name: Patrick Moorhead
posts.text: Azure Cobalt tested.

quoted.text:
Signal65 compared the latest @Azure Cobalt 200 with Cobalt 100, two generations of the custom Arm-based server processor from Microsoft, across four kinds of work.

We ran both generations on the largest general-purpose VM of each and reported results per instance and per vCPU. The Cobalt 200 VM has 1.33x the vCPUs, so the per-vCPU view shows how much of the gain comes from each core. The report also includes EDA chip-design results that Microsoft silicon engineers produced on their own design flows, which Signal65 reviewed.

Key findings from the Lab Insight:

➡️ Cobalt 200 delivered 1.43x to 5.53x the throughput of Cobalt 100 per instance, and 1.07x to 4.15x per vCPU

➡️ Developer and system tasks ran at 1.76x the work per instance on Terminal-Bench 2 in our testing

➡️ Function calling for AI agents reached 1.59x to 1.93x the requests per second per instance, with identical accuracy

➡️ GROMACS molecular dynamics rose 1.43x to 1.46x per instance

➡️ RTL simulation for chip design completed 3.43x to 5.53x the jobs per hour per instance, in tests run by Microsoft silicon engineers and reviewed by Signal65

➡️ A fleet sized for a fixed load needs roughly 30% to 48% fewer instances on the developer, agentic AI and HPC workloads we tested

Read the full Lab Insight: https://signal65.com/research/azure-cobalt-200-outperforms-cobalt-100-per-instance-and-per-core/

CHINA 🇨🇳 SEEKS TO RESTART U.S. PRIVATE EQUITY INVESTMENTS: FT

China's sovereign wealth fund, China Investment Corporation, is negotiating terms with private equity firms that would allow Chinese investors to recover their money if U.S. or European sanctions are imposed, without forcing funds to sell their assets.

Proposals include repayment arrangements tied to fund exits, separate investment vehicles and provisions allowing investors to opt out of individual deals.

Chinese state-backed investors stopped making new U.S. private equity commitments during last year's trade war, after previously backing firms including Blackstone, Carlyle, Thoma Bravo and Vista Equity.

Fund advisers say Trump's recent China visit helped revive CIC's interest, although no new investment commitments have been announced.

Poland’s post-1989 economic transformation remains an unbelievable success, a shift from a poor socialist economy to a large, export-oriented market that has approached Western living standards, surpassed $1 trillion in GDP, and often outpaced most of the EU. Extending this model further without friction is less certain though. Let’s take a look:

Demographics pose the most immediate pressure. Fertility is at postwar lows, natural population decline is routine, and the core working-age population is set to shrink by over a million within a decade. Immigration and higher older-worker participation help but do not fully offset the loss. Fewer workers supporting more retirees means slower potential growth, tighter labor markets, and rising pressure on pensions and healthcare. A move to higher retirement age, especially for women, is needed.

posts.text:
每当市场大跌的时候，这种宝典文章都是穿越时空的投资者指南。

如何战胜股市波动的投资者指南

3根阴线改变信仰，预测难执行更难。既然未来不可测波动加大，投资者怎么办？

6月1日上海两千多万人从 Covid 封控中走出来的日子。如果在 2020 年初，有人告诉你，一座中国最国际化的大都市会经历那样的封控、停摆和集体记忆，你会信吗？（订阅者专享｜周报深度 5/31的公开版 他强任他强：尾部事件冲击下的六月买方策略）

这就是尾部事件。

不是因为它一定没人想到，而是因为人在趋势中，总是高估眼前秩序的稳定性，低估极端拐点对现实世界的冲击。
市场也一样。

人类擅长把最近发生的事情外推成未来，却不擅长理解真正的结构性跳变。半导体存储就是例子。2023 年 DRAM 和 NAND 还在周期低谷，市场规模不到千亿美元级别，到了 2026、2027 年，AI 需求和价格周期把整个行业重新推到完全不同的量级。你让分析师在低谷线性预测十倍变化，很多模型都没有意义。

所以本周的标题是金庸那句话：

他强任他强，清风拂山岗。

外部越乱，越要有自己的内在秩序。

但这里的“坚定”，不是无脑 all in，不是喊口号，也不是抱着一个股票谈恋爱。真正的坚定，来自你知道自己该看什么，知道什么变量在改变，知道什么价格已经包含了什么预期，知道仓位该如何承受尾部事件冲击。

核心就看三件事：
分子、分母、仓位纪律。

posts.text:
Bending Spoons just bought Mailchimp for $3.68 billion. Intuit paid $12 billion for it in 2021.

Mailchimp actually got the best price of the five big names Bending Spoons has bought, measured against each one’s peak valuation:

- Miro: $17.5B peak (Jan 2022). Sold for about $1.79B. 10 cents on the dollar.
- Vimeo: $7.2B at its 2021 spin-off. Sold for $1.38B. 19 cents.
- Airtable: $11B peak (Dec 2021). Sold for about $2.25B. 20 cents.
- Eventbrite: $1.76B at its 2018 IPO. Sold for $500M. 28 cents.
- Mailchimp: $12B in 2021. Sold for $3.68B. 31 cents.

None of these companies were DOA. They’re big, well-known, mostly recurring businesses with millions of customers. They stopped growing, and in 2026 a big B2B company that isn’t growing sells for 2-3x revenue.

Mailchimp is guiding to 0% growth this year on about $1.26B of revenue. In 2021 it was growing 20% on $800M, which is how it got 15x.

If you run a B2B company growing under 10%, these five deals are your comps now, not your last round. Bending Spoons will pay for cash flow it can squeeze, and a reorg comes with the check.

quoted.text:
🚨 OUR MODEL COULD NOT FIND A CLEAN MATCH FOR THIS SELLOFF. 

That may be the most important finding.

We searched every 12-session SPY and QQQ window since 2003 for the current sequence:

A crash from near the highs

A fast rebound

Several quiet sessions on light volume

A second breakdown on rising volume

The closest price paths failed the test because none contained a 4% to 6% crash on three times normal volume.

This pattern is genuinely rare.

So we changed the question.

What historically happened when SPY:

Fell at least 3.5% on twice normal volume

Rebounded

Closed below the crash-day close within 5 to 15 sessions

Only six prior episodes qualified.

Twenty sessions after the breakdown:
SPY average: -5.6%
SPY median: -2.2%
QQQ average: -4.3%

Four of six SPY cases finished lower.

Compared with randomly selected high-volatility periods, the SPY result produced a resampled p-value of 0.041. QQQ produced p = 0.067.

But the sample is only six, and the conventional SPY t-test was not significant at p = 0.26.

The outcomes split into three groups:

2007 and 2025: the breakdown was the low or close to it.

2010 and 2011: several more weeks of weakness, followed by recovery.

2008 and 2020: the breakdown started another 17% to 25% decline.

The 60-session result offered no reliable edge:

SPY median: +5.3%

Positive cases: four of six

The most relevant comparison may be 2007.

It was the only prior case where the initial crash began near an all-time high, as this one did

The most relevant comparison may be 2007.

It was the only prior case where the initial crash began near an all-time high, as this one did. The breakdown close became the low, and SPY later reached new highs.

That is one observation, not a forecast.

The variable separating the recoveries from the disasters was continued selling pressure.

In 2008 and 2020, volume kept expanding after the breakdown.

This time, SPY volume increased from 0.85 times average to 1.7 times over the past four sessions, but it remains well below the three-times-average volume recorded on November 5.

Tomorrow is OPEX.

A high-volume reversal would move the current setup toward the 2007, 2025 and November 2025 recovery templates.

Selling volume exceeding the November 5 level without a reversal would move it toward the 2008 and 2020 group.

The model does not say the bottom is in.

It says the market has reached the decision point that separated historical bottoms from historical crashes.

Tomorrow’s volume may tell us which path we are on.

Historically, that has been bullish later,

The entire VIX term structure is backwardated:
VIX9D: 29.26

VIX6M: 26.85

VIX divided by VIX3M is now 1.052, higher than 97% of readings since 2009.

This is the third consecutive day of backwardation.

How rare is that?

The curve has been backwardated on only 329 of 4,320 trading days since 2009, or 7.6% of the sample.

We tested what happened next.

On historical episodes resembling today, with the ratio between 1.00 and 1.10 and VIX between 24 and 34:

SPY after 21 sessions:
Average return: +2.58%
Positive: 72%
Statistically significant: p = 0.007

SPY after 63 sessions:
Average return: +6.84%

QQQ after 21 sessions:
Average return: +2.55%
Positive: 66%
Not statistically significant: p = 0.11

QQQ after 63 sessions:
Average return: +9.70%
The catch is the path.

On the third day of a backwardation episode, the following session averaged:
SPY: -0.27%
QQQ: -0.49%

The typical worst drawdown during the following month was:
SPY: -2.6%
QQQ: -4.1%

In one of every 10 comparable episodes, the drawdown reached roughly:
SPY: -7.1%
QQQ: -8.5%

Backwardation is not a timing signal. It is a regime signal. The next two closes matter.

If the curve quickly returns to contango, this was another short volatility flare-up.

If backwardation persists and the ratio moves above 1.10, the market is entering a deeper stress regime.

Fear has reached a historically unusual level.

Historically, that improved the opportunity.

It did not eliminate the volatility required to capture it.

posts.name: Diane Swonk
posts.text:
Sitting on a One-Legged Stool?

The economy bent. It didn’t break. The AI boom and the wealth it generated kept it going, but concentrated gains in the hands of a few firms and households. The result was a resilience that failed to resonate for too many.

Now the AI trade is wobbling and our strength is our vulnerability. It is akin to sitting on a one-legged stool. Alfred Nobel, yes, of Nobel Prize fame, used a one to keep his workers from nodding off while mixing nitroglycerin. 🤯

The same wealth gains that helped sustain consumer spending can become a vulnerability when markets correct. The narrower the source of resilience, the greater the exposure when it weakens. Escalating inequality is both a social and economic liability.

Bubbles and technological innovation have long been uneasy companions. History is littered with them. Canals, railroads, electrification and the tech boom of the 1990s are all examples. 

Investors front-run the promise. Capital floods in. Infrastructure gets built. Innovation can endure, even if the investment boom often doesn’t.

Backlogs are large. Demand hasn’t disappeared. Speculative players will get knocked out along the way.

That’s a shakeout but it does not guarantee a soft landing. My worry is what happens if a correction grows tentacles, moving from equities into credit and ultimately the broader economy.

Then there are the vulnerabilities in the technology itself. The rush to harness AI’s capabilities is being matched by a rush to patch vulnerabilities in our systems.

Necessary? Absolutely. 
Reassuring? Hardly.

Innovation requires technology; productivity growth requires trust, which we are lacking. People need to believe their fortunes will rise with the tide, not recede with the shore.

What plays well in Silicon Valley isn’t sitting well on Main Street. Wall Street is getting uncomfortable, too. That is a lot of weight to put on one leg.

My fear isn’t simply that the AI trade corrects. It is that a correction reveals just how much of the economy’s resilience has come to depend on the wealth and investment the boom created.

Resilience that doesn’t resonate could become a reckoning. It is hard living in my head these days. 
Reupping the link to my bear market scenario. Unclear how much wiggle room the Federal Reserve will have to step in and cut, given tail on backlogs and supply chains problems.

posts.name: CtheLightTrading
posts.text:
THE COUNT 📌

Today marks the 3rd 80%+ downside breadth day in 11 sessions: Nov 5, Nov 12, and today.

Nov 5 snapped a 243-session streak without one—the longest in at least 30 years. History shows they rarely come alone: in 11 of the 15 prior cases since 1996, at least one more followed within 30 sessions.

Drawdowns from 52-week highs so far:

• Nasdaq: -13.9%

• Dow Jones: -10.3% 

• S&P 500: -8.5% (6-day losing streak)

DISTRIBUTION OR CAPITULATION?
Three 80%+ downside days in a tight cluster point to two paths:

• Capitulation: sellers flush out in waves, answered by an 80–90% UPSIDE breadth day within sessions

• Distribution: weak bounces, lower highs, and continued institutional selling

What leans capitulation:

• Record-negative dealer gamma (forced mechanical selling)

• Stretched oversold readings & heavy hedging demand

What leans distribution:

• Fundamental headwinds (AI capex ROI scrutiny, hawkish Fed 50 bps hike talk, Middle East tensions)

• Broken key support (Dow <50k) lacking dip-buyers

The tell: Watch for an 80–90% upside breadth day over the next few sessions. Without it, bounces remain suspect.

My primary weekly count suggests GLD is working through a larger Wave 4 correction following the completion of Wave 3.

I've currently labeled Wave 4 as an A-B-C zigzag, but that doesn't mean the correction must end in three waves. Wave 4 can develop into a more complex corrective structure, including a combination or triangle.

Look back at Wave 2. It spent considerable time moving sideways before the next major advance began. Wave 4 could also consume time rather than simply correcting through price.

Key support: $305–$336. This is the zone I'm watching for potential completion of Wave 4.

If the structure confirms, the larger roadmap still allows for a Wave 5 advance. But that remains a scenario, not a confirmed reversal.

Remember, these are weekly candles. Larger Elliott Wave structures don't unfold overnight. A correction of this degree can take several months or even a year to complete. There is no reason to rush the count, force a bottom, or assume the next impulsive advance is just around the corner.

Hope it helps. Thanks.

Elon Musk explains why SpaceX catching Starship achieves the "holy grail of rocketry," and can cut the cost of access to space by 100x:

In 2025, SpaceX launched 2,200 tons to orbit, more than 80% of the global total.

Elon Musk's goal with Starship is 1,000,000 tons to orbit per year, about 450x what SpaceX launched last year.

Falcon 9 reuses its booster but throws away the upper stage on every flight. Starship is designed to bring back both.

"We've had three booster catches, but this is the first ship catch, which means we've now at least proven that all parts of Starship can be flown to space and recovered in good enough shape to be reflown."

"No one has ever taken a stage like that and created a truly reusable upper stage, and certainly not brought it back and had it land propulsively while being caught by giant chopsticks, which sounds like some kind of preposterous sci-fi book or something. But it's done."

"Starship can drop the cost of access to space by a factor of 100... and achieve a mass to orbit rate that is in the million ton per year range."

"This has been the holy grail of rocketry from the beginning, to have a fully reusable rocket system."

"The Space Shuttle was partially reusable, but the main tank… was thrown away on every flight… The shuttle orbiter, the plane-like thing, would take something like nine months to refurbish between flights."

"Whereas Starship is designed for complete reusability and to be reused immediately like an airplane. The booster lands, you can put another ship on top and take off immediately."

"The net effect of this, to put it into economic terms, is a hundredfold reduction in the cost of access to space, and maybe even eventually a thousandfold reduction."

"That's what's necessary in order to make life multiplanetary, in order to build a city on the Moon or Mars… You couldn't do it even if you had the whole budget of the United States government."

Elon Musk and SpaceX have been working toward a fully reusable orbital rocket for more than two decades.

Five days ago, they proved every part of Starship can fly to space and be recovered.

posts.text:
🔔 The Daily Semi-Cap — November 19, 2026

📊 SMH: $447.48 (-2.62% vs prior trading close)

• TSMC halted affected Chinese chip orders on 16nm and more advanced processes unless customers secure U.S. export licenses. Chinese designers generally face a fallback to 28nm/40nm without HBM or advanced packaging. The tightening closes another manufacturing route for domestic AI accelerators; Samsung also suspended some Chinese shipments.

• California served Nvidia an investigative subpoena over whether advanced chips or confidential information reached China and whether investors were misled. This adds a state-level securities investigation to the company’s leadership and export-control problems. It is an information-gathering step, not a finding that Nvidia violated the law.

• AMD fell 7.72% after Hunterbrook disclosed a short position and alleged newer AMD firmware kept reaching blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT. AMD says the claims misrepresent its business and that it complies with export controls. Firmware appearing in a server is not itself proof of an illegal chip shipment.

• Keysight’s fiscal Q4 revenue rose 41% to $1.99B, with adjusted EPS of $3.61 and orders up 53% to $2.34B. Commercial communications grew 73%. Q1 revenue guidance of $2.04–2.06B points to continued test-equipment momentum as faster communications and more complex semiconductor designs expand the infrastructure opportunity beyond GPUs.

• Anthropic’s IPO totaled $81.3B at $83 per share, alongside a $26B private placement: $107.3B combined. The financing strengthens a major compute buyer’s balance sheet, but its nearly $900B of computing commitments remain enormous. For infrastructure suppliers, financing contracted capacity still matters as much as announcing customer demand.

• The IEA’s new World Energy Outlook puts data-center electricity use around 1,000TWh by 2030 in its stated-policies scenario, roughly double today’s level. Connection queues in several regions already exceed current peak demand. Copper, cable and transformer constraints make grid delivery—not simply ordering more accelerators—a critical limit on monetizing AI capacity.

Jensen out at Nvidia, Anthropic's $1.4T IPO, HubSpot brings back Halligan, and Microsoft 365 down for two days.

#1 Anthropic will hit $100B in revenue with under 6,000 employees

**Closing Brief — Thu Nov 19**

● S&P 500 7,175.83 (-2.02%) — sixth straight down day
● Nasdaq 23,879.20 (-2.25%)
● Dow 49,097.06 (-2.19%, -1,101 pts) — closed below 50,000

**What happened**
● Stocks attempted to rally right out of the gate, but the effort quickly faltered. There really wasn't a lot of incremental news on Thursday specifically, and many of the reasons cited for the pressure could have been said at any time in the last few weeks
● Among the more popular justifications for the ugly price action: 1) a hawkish Fed — the FOMC is guaranteed to hike on 12/9, probably again on 1/27 and maybe 3/17 too, as it tries to wrap its arms around an inflation problem that's worse than anticipated; 2) Iran uncertainty — NYT, Axios and Bloomberg all ran "Trump is considering another bombing campaign" stories, although oil took it in stride and didn't really rally, with global markets in a state of oversupply; 3) continued AI doubts — the Anthropic IPO was impressive, but the overall pool of capital available to finance data centers remains smaller than before, while incremental restrictions on chip sales to China are already having an impact on the industry
● 4) poor economic data — the Philadelphia Fed report pointed to cooling growth and intensifying inflation; 5) US government shutdown risks — a shutdown is possible as soon as 12/11; 6) cybersecurity fears — every day brings a new wave of cyber-attack and IT-outage headlines, and they're starting to weigh on the market; 7) blah retail earnings — WMT was OK with a modest beat-and-raise, but BBWI and WSM each provided cautious guidance for Q4
● Sentiment as of the 4pm close was particularly bleak — SPX below its 200-day and sitting at multi-month lows, most people abandoning hope for a year-end rally. The midterms, Nvidia earnings and Ant's IPO don't appear to have been the clearing events many anticipated, and it's difficult to envision a catalyst to propel a dramatic turnaround, with AI-linked stuff still in the penalty box while defensives are extended and expensive

TOM LEE: “IT FEELS LIKE MAX PAIN”

Tom Lee @fundstrat believes the technology selloff is a healthy correction, not the end of the AI boom.

He compares today's market to Cisco in 1997, when shares plunged nearly 50% before a dramatic recovery.

But his most interesting argument concerns who funds AI's next expansion.

The security risks uncovered by Jensen Huang's affair and dealings with companies in and around China could further restrict money flows in the sector at large, via regulatory pressures on the industry and export restrictions on its products.  In our Chart of the Week on November 13th, we pointed out that Congress could attempt to tighten export controls given the news that Nvidia chips were illegally making their way to China. Based on publicly filed data, 6% of the company’s revenue could be impacted in such a worst-case scenario. This figure likely understates sales to the country given the possibly illicit nature of the dealings and indirect sales to China through Southeast Asia. Nonetheless, any curtailment of the significant portion of Nvidia’s revenue and subsequently cash flows that comes from China sales might dent company efforts to fund other areas of the AI buildout. 
 
Likewise, tighter export restrictions could have a material impact on overall index, semiconductor, and AI supplier revenues. Currently, a relatively small 2.3 percentage points of S&P 500 revenue growth is expected to come from China in 2027. However, 21.7 and 13.7 percentage points of the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) and AI supplier’s topline growth is forecast to come from China next year. Even if all revenues from China vanished, estimates imply the SOX would still post 29.7% sales growth next year. While this is still extremely robust, it would mark a sharp deceleration from 2026’s 68.6% pace. Removing all disclosed China revenue would likewise drop the S&P 500 and AI suppliers 2027 topline growth rate by roughly 2.3 and 13.7 percentage points, landing them at 6.5% and 29.3% growth respectively, a material slowdown from 13.4% and 66.3% growth in 2026.

posts.text:
A quick take on Anthropic’s IPO and how it ties in with OpenAI. 

Anthropic made history today, and I think it’s safe to say the IPO was a success across the board. Its fully diluted valuation reached about $2 trillion at the start of trading. Shares opened at $111.50, 34.3% above the $83 IPO price, and stayed above the IPO price in subsequent trading.

Anthropic got everything it could have hoped for from its IPO and expects $104.8 billion in net proceeds from the IPO and the concurrent private placement. That’s fresh capital it needs and plans to use, in particular, to keep leasing data centers. That makes SpaceXSI an indirect beneficiary. In other words, Anthropic’s IPO is a win for both Anthropic and SpaceX.

OpenAI is the loser here. And even if a lot of people don’t want to hear it, I think it needs to be said. OpenAI lost in this case regardless (!) of whether GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol really are that bad or have gotten significantly better since then. The reason is that Anthropic’s IPO achieved what OpenAI is aiming for. With its IPO, Anthropic has gained a head start in terms of financing and established a public valuation benchmark against which OpenAI will be measured should it pursue an IPO of its own. That’s a fact.

The stronger OpenAI had looked ahead of the IPO and the more convincingly it had shown investors that it was the real play, the less money would have gone into Anthropic and the more capital would be available to OpenAI next year. That’s what matters.

The two are each other’s biggest competitors, and I can’t imagine a scenario in which OpenAI didn’t try, at least in some way, to undercut Anthropic’s valuation by putting out a release two days before Anthropic’s IPO. I think it’s pretty clear that it didn’t work. And (again) it makes no difference whether OpenAI’s model is good or bad.

What was disastrous about the release was the public perception. The impression was that it wasn’t a good release, and the market bore that out. As the IPO numbers show, it posed no threat to Anthropic.

If anything, it went the other way. In my view, OpenAI’s latest release probably hurt OpenAI and strengthened Anthropic, because for a lot of people, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 are still the best models even after the release. And yes, I know Astra leads in many areas, including science. That carries little weight with the market or in the public eye. That’s how this IPO should be put in context. And that’s how the numbers should be read.

Big day for Anthropic, a lot of work for OpenAI. But the end is still open.

Palmer Luckey explains why he wants Jensen Huang back at Nvidia despite opposing chip exports to China

“What I said is that China wants Jensen out, so I want him in. And to be clear, I don’t actually agree with Jensen on very material ideas that he has about what the U.S. relationship should be with the Chinese economy. I don’t think that we should be exporting chips to China. He thinks that there’s an argument. I think these are reasonable arguments. There’s other smart people I know, including in the administration, who agree with them. I just happen to not be quite on their side.”

“There’s a lot of people who hear that, and it’s like the midwit take. They say, ‘Palmer, Nvidia is the one that was helping China. So you’re an idiot.’ And what they don’t understand is China doesn’t want Nvidia to sell GPUs to Chinese companies. There are Chinese companies that want to buy Nvidia GPUs. There’s 600,000 H200 GPUs sitting in a port right now because China will not give them an import permit, because they want to build an internal domestic processor industry, silicon industry, not build one that is dependent on the United States.”

“And so the point that I’ve made is China is thrilled to have Jensen, who is somebody who is pro-selling into—and they’ll say, ‘But Jensen was helping smuggle into China.’ Yes, against the Chinese government’s will. The bizarre thing that people don’t get is Jensen was basically on the side of Chinese AI companies, but not the Chinese government. And so they’re thrilled to have Jensen out. And they know this also: there’s a reason it’s knocking a trillion dollars off Nvidia’s market cap. They know that it makes America weaker to knock him out.”

“And I’m sure this CFO lady, they put it as interim CEO, is a perfectly wonderful woman, but she is not Jensen, and she is not going to lead them into a period of prosperity that persists for a millennium. It’s just, she’s not quite the right person. Jensen is the guy who built this company from scratch. He deeply understands it. His personal relationships are the reasons that everyone is willing to do business, because paper means nothing. Paper gives you the right to sue somebody after you think they screwed you. That doesn’t actually solve problems. A piece of paper that says I can sue the guy who screwed me, it doesn’t actually solve the issue.”

“Nobody can take Jensen’s place in this critical juncture. And so again, China wants him out. Therefore I want him in. But he shouldn’t have slept with whatever she turns out to be.”

posts.name: Cullen Roche
posts.text:
Nobody disputes that reserves are a Fed liability and a bank asset. The question is whether that makes my deposit a claim on the Fed. It doesn’t. Claims aren’t transitive. A creditor of a creditor isn’t a creditor. If I own Apple stock and Apple owns Treasuries I don’t have a claim on the Treasury. Your depositor → bank → Fed chain describes how settlement works. It doesn’t describe who owes what to whom.

The test is what happens when the bank fails. If depositors had a claim that ended at the Fed, they’d go to the Fed. They don’t. Insured depositors go to the FDIC. Uninsured depositors go to the receivership and line up with the other creditors. At IndyMac in 2008 the uninsured depositors got a 50% advance dividend to start. That’s what it looks like when your claim is on a bank and not on the central bank. Par isn’t something the Fed owes you. It’s a bank promise backed by the bank’s assets, deposit insurance, regulation and the bank’s access to Fed lending. Those things make par very reliable. They don’t move your claim to the Fed.

Your collateral point actually makes my case. Treasury insists on collateral for balances it leaves at commercial banks because its claim is on the bank, not the Fed. If a bank deposit were a claim on the Fed, the collateral would be pointless. Treasury requires it because it knows exactly whose liability it’s holding. 

MMT just glosses over all these institutional transactions and hand waves them away with generalizations. Sorry, but it's wrong.

Ex-Viking PM Paul Enright explains how analysts should split their work between themselves and AI

“But if you want to be able to survive and coexist and leverage AI to the best, my suggestion would be take the things that have the longest half-life, that have the greatest ability to get embedded in your long-term working memory, to be crystallized. I know things about Charter Communications, Disney, Qualcomm, Intel that I will never forget.”

“Don’t short-circuit. Don’t take a shortcut and ask AI to summarize a bunch of stuff that you should be doing yourself. You should be reading every single document you can get your hands on. You should be buying books off of Amazon and learning the history. And then, like a CIA agent is my favorite analogy, you should get out into the field and you should be having conversations. You should be walking floors. You should be testing products.”

“The stuff that you want to automate and that you want to give to AI is the stuff that has a pretty short half-life and where it’s a complete waste of your time. Why are you building a spreadsheet that shows what consensus earnings are doing? They’re moving all the time. Automate that.”

“Claude can one-shot a model in a few minutes now. You should decide exactly how you want the model to build up, with the KPIs. Don’t let AI decide what the inputs are, because you won’t understand the inputs. Once it’s up and running, sure, have it update it for you on earnings in 2 seconds. Launching coverage, do it yourself. Maintaining coverage, get the help.”

quoted.text:
Gold is trading near $3,750/oz, its lowest in over a year and down more than 30% from the January peak. Let’s take a look what’s driving that, shall we?

Here are the main reasons for the drop:

• Hawkish Fed signals have markets pricing a near-certain December rate hike, raising the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding gold.

• A strong US dollar (near 19-month highs) and elevated real yields (~3% on TIPS, with 10-year yields around 5%) make yield-bearing assets far more attractive.

• Some selling is positioning-driven as investors raise cash amid broader market volatility.

• Geopolitical tensions have lifted oil and inflation, reinforcing rate-hike bets rather than boosting safe-haven demand.

• Technical breaks below key levels have accelerated the decline.

What’s the mid-term outlook then?

• Near-term pressure is likely to persist while the Fed remains hawkish.

• Banks have cut targets but still expect recovery: Goldman sees ~$4,150 by end-2026 and ~$4,650–$4,800 by end-2027, UBS targets $4,500 by end-2026 and $5,000 by end-2027.

• Central bank buying, resilient ETF holdings, and concerns over debt and fiscal sustainability continue to provide a floor.

• Meaningful upside is more likely once the hiking cycle ends and cuts are priced (expected later in 2027), drawing private and Western ETF demand back in.

Overall, this appears to be a rates-driven correction rather than a structural breakdown, medium-term bias remains constructive on dips for longer-term holde

posts.name: Jeromy Sonne
posts.text:
My biggest hot take right now is I couldn’t be more bearish on the Anthropic IPO for the long term. Like obviously they’ve built an insanely good model but as a business I just don’t see the value in AI accruing to the frontier labs. To be clear not investment advice and I have no position (Nor do I have positions in any other stock for that matter). Succinctly though my issues with it are the following:

-Distillation is never going to stop and candidly its pretty obviously to me legal to retain the data from a product that you pay for. There is no serious long term way to stop this that I can see and at best its a constant game of whackamole. As long as Claude is a model you can use via either app or API it will keep happening and distillation is a fraction of the cost of the training.

-Even if you buy into they’re going to stop offering models and eat SaaS companies and just offer an entire catalog of products this issue doesn’t really go away. If it costs them 0 to produce software then it does for everyone else too.

-They’re not positioned at all for robots and even if they massively expand headcount to go after white collar services businesses that just then balloons costs and they look like every other company plus STILL there is the competition issue that doesn’t go away. Further they don’t fully understand these industries and its entirely possible they end up whiffing and losing tons of money doing some huge rollout.

-If you think that future of robots is really where the value in AI lies I would tend to agree but they can’t product their own robots so they have to install basically their OS into other people’s devices. The parallels with Apple and the ios store and apps is too strong here and the actual hardware manufacturers always end up winning.

-AI is an insanely powerful piece of tech but the current paradigm of brute force scaling compute tops out pretty quickly and its not clear it can ever get actually efficient especially with all this competition.

-The current LLM based paradigm is strong and can go further but its not clear to me that more “intelligence” is actually the issue or the bottleneck in a lot of industries. It would take a whole new approach imho to make any kind of serious leap and I don’t think machines will ever get to a true human level because (and this sounds wishy washy and hand wavvy hippie style but bear with me) without discernment that comes from context and emotions you’re capped at usefulness. Pure logic only gets you so far. Yes I'm a Yann fanboy in this area. No I don't care.

-Their entire financials are predicated around this notion that they are profitable if you don’t count the cost of training the models. This is the equivalent of saying like Toyota would be profitable if they didn’t develop a new car every year. The idea that a lab can simply stop producing new models is farcical to me because the switching costs between companies is near 0.

-Further as the AI bubble pops or deflates compute is going to get cheaper over the long term plus as manufacturing and data centers continue to ramp and get more efficient the cost for compute keeps dropping in the medium and long term. On the surface this would seem to help them but it really just opens it up for more competition that can train more specialized models easier and faster too.

المفارقة أن الذهب الذي يُفترض أن يحمي المستثمرين من الأزمات بات ضحية لها! ففي وقت تتصاعد فيه المخاطر الجيوسياسية والتضخم والديون السيادية، فقد المعدن الأصفر اكثر من ثلث قيمته منذ ذروته في يناير/ كانون الثاني 2026، متراجعا من 5,595 إلى نحو 3,684 دولارا للأونصة، بالتزامن مع هبوط أسهم التكنولوجيا.

ويمكن أن نعزو هذا التراجع إلى ثلاثة عوامل رئيسية: ارتفاع الفائدة وقوة الدولار بفعل تداعيات الحرب على إيران، وخروج المضاربين الذين ساهموا في صعود الذهب، واضطرار بعض المستثمرين إلى بيعه لتوفير السيولة وتغطية خسائرهم في الأسهم.

أما الاقتصادي روبين بروكس، فيرى أن تراجع الذهب قد يعكس ضغوطا مالية أعمق بفعل تشدد السياسة النقدية الأمريكية وتصاعد المخاوف في الأسواق، وربما يشير إلى بداية موجة أوسع لتقليص المديونية وتصفية المراكز المالية، وإن كان من المبكر الجزم بحدوثها.

وهنا تكمن المفارقة، قد لا يكون الذهب قد فقد مكانته ملاذا آمنا، بل إن المستثمرين يضطرون إلى بيعه عند اشتداد الأزمات لتوفير السيولة. لكن هل يعكس تراجعه انتكاسة مؤقتة، أم أن ارتباطه المتزايد بتقلبات الأسواق بدأ يقوّض دوره التقليدي في تنويع المحافظ الاستثمارية والتحوط من المخاطر؟

posts.name: Fireside Alpha
posts.text:
Anthropic board member & Novartis CEO pushes back on Dario’s “less than a decade” cancer prediction: “cure is a big word”

He says, though, AI could cut drug development from 12 years to 8

EISEN (ANCHOR): “Can a frontier lab, do you think, eventually cure cancer?”

VAS NARASIMHAN (CEO): “I think this is going to happen in stages. You and I have talked about this in the past. What we’re going to first see is an acceleration in our timelines. Today I outlined in our capital markets day, it takes around twelve years from when we find a potential drug to when we get it to patients. And I think AI is going to help us get that over time from twelve years down to eight years. And then when you think about how many diseases we can tackle, there’s only about ten to fifteen percent of diseases today that have meaningful medicines. So can AI help us discover more potential medicines to treat patients over a decade and beyond? I think absolutely.”

“And then step by step, we’ll also hopefully increase the probability of success that these medicines work. In our industry today, the industry average is only eight percent of a medicine getting into the clinic that can work. If we can just move that to twelve percent, that’s already a huge gain for how we actually find these medicines. So I think taken together, we’re going to get there. I think as a clinician, cure is a big word, so I always want to be careful. I think we can get meaningful therapies, many more meaningful therapies, to patients in the next decade, for sure.”

QUINTANILLA (ANCHOR): “It sounds a little more circumspect, Vas, than Amodei himself, who did say, and I’m quoting: cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease, mental illness, these will be relics of the past in, I think, less than a decade. You’re not quite going there.”

NARASIMHAN: “Look, I think as always, the scientists are going to have different opinions, and none of us really know what the answer is. I think the important thing is that it is a noble goal that Dario outlines, and I think we absolutely want to get there as fast as we can. And I think we’re all working towards that. And if we got there, that would be incredible.”

“I just think we also have to be humble in the face of the complexity of human biology. We’re going to have to work through this step by step. And, of course, we want to get there as fast as we can. Look, if it happens in ten years, that would be a remarkable thing, and I’m all for it.”

quoted.text:
Dario Amodei says AI could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade

“Now we can build that intelligence. Whether it’s protein folding, drug design, cancer genetics or clinical trial administration, scientists across many areas of biology and medicine are finding Claude can help them do their research in a fraction of the time it would have taken just a couple of years ago.”

“I believe sufficiently powerful AI working in concert with humans could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade. I don’t want to get ahead of myself. At this point, all we have are early results.”

Dario Amodei says Anthropic could drive at 200 miles an hour but chooses 90

“So this is one of the central tensions at the heart of the company, but it’s really because this technology is so powerful, it has so many effects in the world. It’s something that every company in this space will have to face, whether they want to or not. We’re just facing it more explicitly and more thoughtfully. “The idea behind pacing was, imagine that you’re driving your car at 60 miles an hour, and then you discover or invent something that could let you drive the car at 200 miles an hour. A short report out today calls AMD the Silicon Valley Bank of AI.

We ran AMD’s latest 10-Q through the Alphatica Earnings Quality Signal. It still scores 6/6, and operating income has more than tripled year to date.

But the cushion is thinner. Cash conversion has slipped, receivables and inventory are up about 45%, and long-term debt has tripled.

The reported numbers are clean. The trend is worth watching.

On the export claims: we’re not export lawyers, but here’s what the public record shows. The Commerce rule cited (90 FR 14046) added IEIT Systems to the Entity List effective March 25, 2025. Exports to it need a license, and applications are presumed to be denied.

The rule doesn’t mention AMD or firmware. Whether firmware reaching a listed company is a violation depends on how it got there and whether it was publicly available. That’s a question for regulators, not a data read.

What will it take for tokenization to scale?

CoinShares CEO Jean-Marie Mognetti says giants like BlackRock and DTCC are likely to come together on a common format and unlock scale, interoperability and fungibility

"We are at the cusp of it. 25 years ago, Steve Jobs was jumping on the stage in Cupertino and introducing the iPod."

"Before you got the iPod, you had like 25 different music compression algorithms, all fighting for funding. Then Steve Jobs showed up on the stage and decided, okay, this is going to be the format, and everybody else can get lost."

"We're pretty much on the cusp of the same move, especially in the US. You're probably going to get people like BlackRock, DTCC and BNY coming together and saying, okay, we understand tokenization."

"Tokenization is basically securitization 3.0. It is basically turbocharging distribution for institutions. So they want that, because that's a way to make more money."

"At the same time, they need a common format, not 20 different platforms and 20 different ways to do it. A common format creates fungibility, a common format creates interoperability, and it creates scalability."

Japan after 1989 illustrates precisely that dynamic, as massive fiscal deficits and monetary easing coexisted with declining government bond yields amid prolonged economic stagnation. posts.name: James E. Thorne
posts.text:
A Generational Mistake in the Making
The Fed is preparing to make a historic, generational mistake.

The real policy rate is already 1.93%, well into restrictive territory. Now the base effects are about to tighten it further, with no help from the Fed. Next spring, the war’s energy spike drops out of the inflation numbers. 

Leave policy where it is and the real rate climbs to 2.21% by the end of 2027 even if energy prices only hold flat. If energy returns to its pre-war level, it reaches 3.29%, the highest since 2000. If the energy glut pushes prices 10% below pre-war, inflation falls under 1% and the real rate hits 3.88%, the highest since 1990.
That’s the tightening coming from doing nothing. The Fed wants to hike on top of it.

Core goods inflation is 0.7%. Input prices in the New York Fed’s own survey have plunged. Oil and diesel are falling. Yet the case for hiking rests on anecdotes about AI and a fear of growth, with no evidence offered.

Arthur Burns let inflation run in the 1970s. This Fed is making the opposite mistake: hiking into falling inflation and sending real rates to levels not seen in a generation. History will not be kind.

posts.name: EndGame Macro
posts.text:
COVID Created A False Sense Of Housing Wealth And Reality Is Beginning To Set In

American homeowners are sitting on approximately $35 trillion in housing equity, equivalent to roughly 106% of U.S. GDP, near historical highs. Yet home sales relative to the number of homeowners have fallen to approximately 4.3%, near their lowest levels in decades. This extraordinary divergence reveals a housing market where enormous amounts of wealth exist on paper, but relatively few buyers are willing or financially capable of purchasing properties at current valuations.

How COVID Distorted Housing Values

The pandemic created an extraordinary environment for housing. Mortgage rates collapsed to 2.65%, fiscal stimulus expanded household purchasing power, remote work reshaped demand, and historically limited inventory intensified competition. National home prices surged approximately 42% between early 2020 and mid 2022.

Those who sold during that period converted historically elevated valuations into actual cash. But millions of homeowners who watched neighboring properties sell for extraordinary prices began treating those transactions as permanent benchmarks for their own wealth.

The problem is that the economic conditions supporting those valuations no longer exist.

Mortgage rates have climbed above 7%, dramatically reducing purchasing power. A $500,000 mortgage that cost approximately $2,015 monthly at 2.65% now costs around $3,424 at 7.28%, nearly 70% more for the exact same loan.

Yet many sellers continue expecting prices established when financing was substantially cheaper.

Why the Market Hasn’t Corrected More Aggressively

The primary reason is mortgage lock in. Millions of homeowners secured mortgages near 3%, giving them little financial incentive to sell and replace those loans at today’s rates.

This has simultaneously restricted housing supply and crushed transaction volumes, allowing elevated valuations to persist despite deteriorating affordability.

But there’s an important distinction between what homeowners believe their properties are worth and what buyers can actually afford to pay.

A home is ultimately worth what a qualified buyer is willing and able to pay, not what a neighbor received during an unprecedented period of monetary stimulus and historically cheap financing.

The Coming Repricing

Historically elevated valuations relative to household purchasing power cannot remain disconnected indefinitely. Some normalization can occur through rising wages, economic growth, and lower borrowing costs, but meaningful price corrections become increasingly plausible when demand weakens and sellers lose their ability to wait.

This is where unemployment becomes critical.

As job losses increase, households experience financial pressure, relocations become necessary, estates are liquidated, and more homeowners may be forced to accept prevailing market prices rather than wait for their preferred valuations.

Meanwhile, prospective buyers facing employment uncertainty may become even more reluctant to make the largest financial commitment of their lives, regardless of whether mortgage rates decline.

That combination could finally break the standoff between buyers and sellers.

The equity to GDP ratio does not have to mechanically return to its historical average through falling prices alone. But the underlying affordability imbalance eventually requires adjustment.

And that adjustment will not necessarily be uniform. Communities with declining populations, weaker employment prospects, and increasing housing supply could experience substantial depreciation, while desirable areas with limited inventory remain comparatively resilient.

The greatest misconception homeowners may be carrying forward from COVID is that extraordinary pandemic valuations represent a permanent measure of their wealth. Those who sold realized those prices. Those who haven’t may eventually discover that the market they remember no longer exists.

At 95.7% refineries are operating near their limits, not demonstrating that supply constraints have disappeared. The EIA explicitly attributes elevated utilization to global refined product shortages and exceptionally strong diesel margins resulting from disrupted refining capacity in Russia and the Middle East. U.S. refining capacity is actually 4% below 2019 levels, while distillate inventories remain 7% below their 5 year seasonal average.

More revealing, refinery crude inputs actually declined by 129,000 barrels per day last week despite higher utilization. So how exactly does this establish that increasing production is driving prices lower rather than weakening demand coinciding with constrained refining capacity? Running refineries near maximum capacity to compensate for global supply shortages is not evidence that those shortages have been resolved. It’s evidence of how hard the remaining infrastructure is working to meet demand.

posts.text:
Israel was forced this week to make public how much aid it has allowed into Gaza. It is resounding proof that it is committing the crime of genocide.

Since Israel agreed a ceasefire in Gaza just over a year ago, it has broken its commitment – month after month – to allow humanitarian supplies into the enclave.

A freedom of information request from the Haaretz newspaper shows that, since March, the aid trucks entering the enclave have never gotten close to the number Israel agreed was required to address the population’s basic needs.

According to the ceasefire’s terms, Israel was supposed to allow in 18,200 trucks a month, or 600 a day.

Last March, Israel let in only a quarter of that number: 4,779.

In April, only a few hundred more trucks entered. By May, half the agreed number were being allowed into Gaza. In the best month, September, Israel approved just over 13,000 trucks – 30 percent fewer shipments than it had committed to.

That did not mark a turning-point. Last month the figure fell back to just over 6,500, barely more than a third of the promised number.

Over the past eight months, there has been a shortfall of just over 74,000 trucks, representing more than half of the aid even Israel agreed a year ago was necessary to keep the population fed, sheltered and cared for.

The basic supplies the people of Gaza are being deprived of include food, fuel, medicines and medical equipment, as well as materials for building temporary shelters and repairing infrastructure.

Israel’s blockade has led to critical shortages of tents, medicines and disinfectants. Humanitarian organisations also lack the supplies needed to repair water pumps and sewage drainage systems, provide shelters and make safe damaged buildings. Even timber is refused.

The problem has become even more acute in recent weeks – just as Israel has again reduced the number of aid trucks – as winter storms have ripped across Gaza, damaging or washing away tents.

This month, some 40,000 tents, a flimsy shelter to 200,000 Palestinians, were flooded, often with waste water from overwhelmed sewage pits that is causing the further spread of disease for which there are no medicines.

According to the UN, some 150,000 tents – as well as hundreds of thousands of tarpaulins, blankets and mattresses – are stuck outside Gaza, with Israel refusing entry.

posts.name: Leyla
posts.text:
"I'm a private credit analyst at a $15 billion fund.

I've been in the industry for 18 months and already underwritten $2.4 billion in loans.

You could say I'm pretty good at this.

Last year, we financed a software buyout. The company made $12 million in EBITDA.

Adjusted EBITDA was $58 million. Pro forma adjusted EBITDA was $81 million.

Obviously, I used $81 million. What am I, an amateur?

Our $450 million unitranche loan was levered at just 5.6 times.

Great loan, if you ask me. 

My associate asked about free cash flow. Dude. It's a software company.

We priced the loan at SOFR plus 550. Almost 10% yield. Senior secured. Equity-like returns with debt-like risk. 

Six months later, EBITDA missed budget by 38%. The sponsor said it was temporary, and who am I to argue? 

We agreed to PIK half the interest.

Now our loan balance grows every quarter without us putting in another dollar.

You know who understands the power of compounding?

- Warren Buffett!

Last week, some distressed debt guys offered 72 cents for our loan. I literally laughed.

We have it marked at 99. Two independent valuation firms confirmed our valuation. 

These distressed guys think they're so smart.

Anyway, we're putting another $40 million into the company. Super-senior. 

My VP says it primes our existing debt. Whatever. We're first lien on both.

My dad asked what happens if the borrower can't repay. I told him we take the collateral.

He asked what the collateral was. Enterprise value, obviously.

He asked what happens if the enterprise has no value.

Jesus Christ.

This is why I don't take financial advice from my parents. He works at a bank. I make three times what he makes, and I'm only 26.

Anyway, I just got promoted."

posts.name: Cullen Roche
posts.text:
Having the right to instruct a payment isn’t the same as having a claim on the asset used to settle it. When you pay taxes you instruct your bank to pay the Treasury. Reserves move because the Treasury banks at the Fed. Under the old TT&L system they often didn’t move at all. And if your bank fails before sending the payment, you still owe the tax and your claim is against the bank. That’s the whole point. Your rights run to the bank. The bank’s obligations run to the Fed. 

Some MMT people frame this as having a claim on the Fed and Central Bank money. You do not.

posts.name: Lewis Bollard
posts.text:
I ate cultivated chicken last night. Before dinner, we toured the @UPSIDEFoods facility — what critics call the "lab" where "lab meat" is made.

What struck me most was how clean it was. Every chicken and pig factory I’ve entered has been filthy, with the pungent smell of manure the animals live on top of.

The Upside facility was spotless. The plant manager told me that in two years of operating they haven’t had a single case of Salmonella or Campylobacter.

By contrast, the most recent USDA testing found Salmonella in 35% of ground chicken and Campylobacter in 25% of whole chicken carcasses from factory farms.

This won’t be for everyone. If you only want "natural" meat, eat pasture-raised meat instead.

But for the majority already eating factory chicken daily, this could be a major upgrade: the same product, minus the pathogens and the cruelty.

posts.name: James E. Thorne
posts.text:
The Fed has a new villain: growth

Expect the Federal Reserve to move the goalposts. For eight months its case for tightening rested on energy. 

That case is collapsing. In October, US producer prices for crude petroleum fell 10.3 per cent and diesel fell 7.9 per cent. Brent is down a third from its April peak, and base effects will drag headline inflation lower through the spring.

So a new rationale has appeared. Vice-chair Philip Jefferson says the AI buildout is “exerting upward pressure on demand and inflation”. New York Fed president John Williams says AI investment and stock market wealth may mean “we need to raise rates more”. In plain terms, growth is now bad.

True to form, the Fed offers anecdotes rather than evidence. Semiconductor producer prices are down 2.7 per cent from a year earlier. IT goods are deflating. Monthly computer price rises have slowed from 3.8 per cent in August to 0.5 per cent in October. 

Bloomberg Economics finds that AI-driven inflation has peaked, and productivity is up 2.1 per cent.
Investment that expands capacity is disinflationary. A central bank that treats prosperity as overheating is no longer dependent on data. It is in search of a justification.

Dustin Moskovitz gave major early money to both OpenAI and Anthropic, but is now super worried that he helped create the machine that ends the world.
